analysis.one_liner: Phases in overtime pay for agricultural workers and ends their exemptions from federal labor law.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 11 Senate sponsors, the bill was referred to committee and received no hearing, no vote, and no further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law has exempted farmworkers from overtime pay since the 1930s, even though most other hourly workers earn it. This bill would require farms and agriculture-related businesses to pay time-and-a-half after a set number of hours, stepping down from 55 hours a week in 2019 to a standard 40-hour week by 2022. Small farms with 25 or fewer employees would get extra years to comply, and workers who are members of the owner's family would remain exempt. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Agricultural workers, one of the lowest-paid and most heavily migrant workforces in the country, would gain the right to overtime pay after a standard workweek, the same protection most other hourly workers have had for decades. Workers in related industries that are currently exempt, such as cotton ginning, sugar processing, and small irrigation operations, would also gain coverage.

how_it_helps.text: Beginning in 2019, farm employers would owe time-and-a-half for hours beyond 55 per week, dropping to 50 in 2020, 45 in 2021, and 40 in 2022, the same threshold other workers have [S2] [S3].
Small farms with 25 or fewer employees would have until 2022 to start paying overtime and until 2025 to reach the full 40-hour week, easing the transition for the smallest operations [S2] [S3].

The bill repeals overtime exemptions for agriculture-related industries including certain small farms, irrigation projects, sugar processing, and cotton ginning and compressing, extending protections to workers the current law leaves out [S2].
Family members of the farm owner would stay exempt, as under current law, preserving the traditional family-farm arrangement [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Farm operators and agriculture-related businesses, including cotton gins, sugar processors, and irrigation operators, would bear higher payroll costs, either by paying overtime, shortening hours, or hiring more workers. Some of that cost would likely pass through to food prices, and small farms were given delayed deadlines in recognition of that burden.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes real payroll costs on farm employers, who operate on thin margins and face price pressure from imported produce; some operators would cut hours, mechanize, or raise prices to absorb it [S2].
Even after full phase-in, the smallest farms would not reach the 40-hour overtime threshold until 2025, so low-wage workers on those farms would wait years for equal treatment [S3].
The bill addresses overtime only; it does not touch other gaps in farmworker labor protections such as union organizing rights or housing standards.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is straightforward: the same overtime protection nearly every other hourly worker has, extended to a workforce with some of the lowest pay and longest hours in the country. The costs fall on farm employers and, indirectly, on food prices, and the bill's long phase-in for small farms acknowledges that burden while delaying relief for some of the workers who most need it. On balance the trade favors the workers, who currently have no overtime right at all.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Kamala Harris introduced the bill on June 25, 2018, joined by 10 cosponsors (9 Democrats and 1 Independent) [S1] [S3] [S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it the same day to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which was its last recorded action [S5].
No hearing, committee vote, or floor action followed before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and bills not passed by the end of a Congress die [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Farm operators and agriculture-related employers are better off because the bill died: they continue to pay no overtime after 55, 50, or 40 hours, as they have since the 1938 exemption was written. Farmworkers remain the losers.

for.name: Sen. Kamala Harris
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 10 Senate cosponsors

for.role: Cosponsors (9 Democrats, 1 Independent, including Feinstein, Booker, Warren, and Sanders)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; none of the cosponsorship included any Republicans

against.name: Senate HELP Committee (Chair Lamar Alexander)
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican senator
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action; no hearing or committee vote was ever scheduled

sides.party_line_note: All 11 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or Independents; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-chaired committee of referral took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would end the 1938-era exemption that lets farm employers pay no overtime regardless of hours worked, raising their payroll costs. Their interest in blocking it runs directly against the wage interest of farmworkers.

industries.industry: Cotton ginning, sugar processing, and irrigation operators
industries.note: These agriculture-related employers hold specific overtime exemptions that the bill repeals, so their workers would newly qualify for time-and-a-half.

industries.industry: Small family farms (25 or fewer employees)
industries.note: They would eventually face the same overtime requirement but with delayed deadlines (overtime starting 2022, full 40-hour week in 2025) in recognition of their smaller margins.
